Tropical Storm Edouard is really starting to look much more organized on radar, with banding on the radar showing up and a buildup of thunderstorms as it heads towards the Texas and Louisiana coastlines. It is going to try to make a run at strong Tropical Storm status, or maybe even Hurricane Status, before landfall this evening. It should make landfall somewhere between High Island, Texas, and Cameron, Louisiana. Hurricane Watches are in place now. 

It’s been fascinating to watch this develop in real time. I was keeping track overnight and, can’t lie, I thought about catching a quick flight to Houston to experience it. 

A Storm Surge Warning is in effect for High Island, Texas to the Vermilion/Cameron Parish Line
 
A Hurricane Watch is in effect for High Island, Texas to Cameron, Louisiana
 
A Tropical Storm Warning is in effect for Port Bolivar, Texas to the Vermilion/Iberia Parish Line

Little storms can be sneaky; thankfully, it has limited time left over warm ocean waters of the Northern Gulf, or else this would definitely be a Hurricane.

items.author: EdPiotrowskiWPDE
items.text:
This photo is a microcosm of what our lives looked like over the last few years before Mom passed.

As many of you know, her health was not great so she spent a lot of time in and out of hospitals, rehab facilities and doctors’ offices. One of her longer stays away from home was at Brightwater, where she went for rehab after surgery to repair a broken tibia.

We visited her every single day for several months. There were times when it was mentally and physically exhausting, but Mom thrived when we were there. She was always so happy to see us, and no matter how tired we might have been, seeing her smile had a way of reinvigorating us.

Looking back now, I realize just how precious those days were.

There were so many great conversations, so much laughter and a lot of reminiscing about when we were kids, and how Mom somehow managed to put up with all four of us. At the time, they were simply visits. Today, they’re memories I wouldn’t trade for anything.

This photo gives a whole new meaning to simply sitting on the porch and relaxing. Whenever we could, we’d get Mom out of her room and into the fresh air. Nothing fancy. Just sitting together, talking and enjoying each other’s company.

I guess all of this is to say that some of life’s most meaningful moments don’t happen in the places or circumstances we would choose. Even in places that are far from ideal or normal, wonderful and lasting memories can be made.

Sometimes you don’t realize just how special those ordinary moments are until you’d give anything to have one more of them.
❤️❤️

TROPICS | Edouard is a compact storm south of the Louisiana coast this morning. There has been a notable increase of showers & storms around the center of the system over the last several hours. This matches well with the NHC's expected strengthening of the system before landfall later today. 

Current winds are around 40 mph but the NHC believes the system may have 60-70 mph winds by the time it reaches the southeast Texas coast midday today. Landfall is most likely near Beaumont. 

The wind or surge will not be major issues with this storm. Only a few isolated spots will actually see strong winds. 

The biggest issues with systems like this is rain. Rainfall totals generally of 3-6" are likely with some spots getting 4-8"+ in the heaviest rain bands. 

My main concern is that much of the heaviest rain will fall overnight in parts of east & southeast Texas. Overnight flooding is a serious concern as those who are traveling overnight will have a difficult time spotting flooded roadways. If you can, alter your plans to travel during the daylight hours as much as possible to make the trip a bit easier.  

The remnants of Edouard will weaken quickly as they drift NW on Wednesday, with most of the storm gone by Thursday, falling apart somewhere near Waco, well south of Dallas/Ft. Worth.

NEW 4AM INFO FOR #EDOUARD
 
NHC remarks about environmental conditions being quite favorable for intensification while Edouard remains over the warm water with very low wind shear. 

The raw output from the hurricane-regional models 
responded to these factors by showing substantial intensification today, with both HMON and HAFS-A making Edouard a hurricane before landfall.

🍁HELLO, FALL!🍁

Well, meteorological fall, that is! It officially begins today. Astronomical fall, on the other hand, won’t kick in until September 22nd. So why the difference?

Astronomical seasons are tied to Earth’s position relative to the sun, while meteorological seasons follow the annual temperature cycle. In weather terms, winter is the three coldest months (Dec–Feb), summer the three hottest (Jun–Aug), with spring (Mar–May) and fall (Sep–Nov) bridging the gap.

And honestly? This is my favorite time of year. After sweating through a hot, sticky summer, I am more than ready for some crisp, dry, refreshing air.

☄️ A quiet meteor shower with a wild streak peaks tonight, capable of surprising us with sudden bursts of fireballs.

The Aurigids reach their peak overnight from August 31 into September 1, normally producing only about 6 meteors per hour. But this shower has a history of rare, dramatic outbursts, briefly flaring to dozens of meteors an hour in years like 2007 and 2021. The debris comes from the long-period comet Kiess, which last visited the inner solar system over a century ago.

🌠 The catch this year is the Moon: a bright waning gibbous, over 80% lit, washing out fainter streaks. Block it behind a building, look toward Auriga rising in the northeast, and watch after midnight. The bright fireballs can still cut through.

items.text: ALL EYES ON LABOR DAY WEEKEND FOR TROPICAL MOISTURE POTENTIAL IN SOCAL & SW🌀🌧️🌊confidence is increasing that tropical moisture will spread north toward California late this week and into the Labor Day Holiday Weekend, but there remains considerable uncertainty over how close the actual tropical system gets to Southern California. Invest 95E, currently a disorganized disturbance well south of Baja California, is expected to develop into Hurricane Marie later this week. The system should initially track northwest toward the waters off Baja California through Friday and Saturday. After that, the forecast becomes much more complicated. The large trough expected across the West Coast will play a major role in determining the eventual track. Ensemble guidance currently shows two primary scenarios: I] one turns the storm farther west and out to sea, II] while the other brings it farther north toward Southern California. Recent ensemble trends favor the farther-west solution, with only around a 5% chance of more direct or significant tropical cyclone impacts to Southern California. That does NOT mean California escapes impacts. Tropical moisture is looking increasingly likely to surge north. Some guidance brings moisture into the Southwest and California as early as Thursday night or Friday, with precipitation chances increasing further Friday through the weekend. Roughly 90% of GEFS and EPS ensemble members increase atmospheric moisture to very high levels across portions of the region by Friday and Saturday. The combination of that moisture and a Pacific trough near the West Coast could provide enough lift for showers and thunderstorms, potentially leading to areas of heavy rainfall. Exactly where and how much rain falls remains uncertain. Ensemble guidance suggests the extreme scenario remains relatively unlikely, with only around 5-10% of roughly 100 projections producing 2+ inches of rain in Southern California. Around 20-30% remain essentially dry, leaving some lighter rainfall as the more likely middle-ground scenario. There is also a low but non-zero chance of stronger easterly winds depending on the eventual track, which could create concerns for fire weather and downed trees. Confidence is higher in coastal impacts. Unless the storm makes a substantial turn westward after Saturday, a strong south swell could affect Southern California through Tuesday. Swells from Hurricane Karina may also still be present, while evening high tides approach 7+ feet by Labor Day Monday. That combination could produce high surf and moderate coastal flooding along south-facing beaches during the busy Labor Day weekend. A closer approach by the tropical system would amplify those impacts. The key message right now: a direct hit is unlikely, but an influx of tropical moisture and coastal impacts are becoming increasingly plausible. There are still plenty of moving pieces, especially since the tropical cyclone hasn't even formed yet. The forecast should become considerably clearer over the next 2-3 days once a defined circulation develops and models get a better handle on its interaction with the Western trough🌀🌧️🌊

Isolated thunderstorms are also possible Wednesday and Thursday, capable of producing brief heavy rain, lightning, gusty winds and small hail. items.text: EARLY-SEASON WIND FOR PNW💨🌲🌧️🍂a strong-for-early-September storm system will move into the Pacific Northwest on Wednesday, bringing widespread rain along with increasingly gusty winds! Across western Washington, western Oregon and northwestern California, the strongest winds are currently favored along the coast and in Washington, the Northwest Interior and San Juans as a cold front approaches and eventually moves through Wednesday into Wednesday night. Although wind alerts may not be issued, this system could still produce more impacts than the numbers alone would suggest. One important factor is that the trees still have their full summer foliage. Leaves significantly increase the surface area exposed to the wind, putting additional stress on branches and entire trees. Combine that with trees already stressed or weakened following a dry summer, and it may take less wind than during a typical late-fall or winter storm to cause problems. As a result, isolated power outages and some downed or broken tree branches will be possible Wednesday, particularly where the strongest gusts occur. A few weakened tree branches could also come down. There remains uncertainty regarding the exact track and strength of the system, which will ultimately determine how strong the winds become. Right now, this does not look like a major Pacific Northwest windstorm, but it is an early-season system worth watching closely because of the increased vulnerability of fully leafed and drought-stressed trees. items.author: EdPiotrowskiWPDE
items.text:
NO HURRICANES YET: 2026 MOVING INTO RARE TERRITORY

It’s the last day of August, and we still haven’t had a hurricane form in the Atlantic. Not that anyone around here is complaining!

As of 2pm on August 31, 2026 ranks 8th for the latest first Atlantic hurricane of the satellite era, which began in 1966. And there’s a very good chance we’re not done climbing the list.

Tropical Storm Eduoard will form soon in the northern Gulf, but make landfall in Texas well below hurricane strength. So, it's a virtual lock that we won’t see a hurricane through Wednesday, which would move 2026 all the way into 5th place. More tropical waves will roll off the African coast over the next several weeks, but for now they’ll be fighting an uphill battle. Hostile wind shear and widespread sinking air, both characteristic of a very strong El Niño pattern, continue to dominate much of the tropical Atlantic. Those conditions make it extremely difficult for tropical systems to thrive.

Perhaps even more remarkable, none of our major forecast models currently develop a hurricane in the Atlantic during the next two weeks. If that forecast holds, 2026 could make a serious run at the record for the latest first hurricane of the modern satellite era: September 11, set by Gustav in 2002 and tied by Humberto in 2013.

There is an interesting historical footnote. The 1907 and 1914 seasons had no hurricanes in the official record, but both occurred long before satellites provided continuous coverage of the Atlantic. Back then, ships were one of the primary ways of discovering storms over the open ocean. A hurricane could form, spend its entire life at sea and dissipate without ever crossing a shipping route. And if ships knew a hurricane was nearby, they generally did their best to avoid it! So comparing those early seasons with today's satellite era isn't exactly apples to apples.

Keep in mind, we're just now entering the climatological peak of Atlantic hurricane season. A quiet start certainly doesn't mean we're in the clear. Mother Nature doesn't care about records or seasonal statistics, and it only takes one hurricane in the wrong place to turn an otherwise quiet season into a devastating one.

items.text: HURRICANE TROPICAL MARIE EXPECTED TO DEVELOP - TROPICAL MOISTURE COULD REACH CALIFORNIA & THE SOUTHWEST⚠️🌀🌧️a developing tropical system well offshore of southwestern Mexico is expected to become Hurricane Marie this week, and it could eventually play an important role in the weather across California and the Southwest during the upcoming Labor Day weekend. The disturbance, currently designated EP95, now has an 80% chance of developing within 48 hours and a 90% chance within seven days. A tropical depression is likely to form within the next couple of days as the system moves generally west-northwest to northwest. Once Marie develops, the system is expected to eventually gain more of a north-to-northwestward component. This could allow tropical moisture associated with the storm to become drawn northward toward California and parts of the Southwest heading into Labor Day weekend. There is increasing confidence that indirect impacts will occur, particularly an increase in tropical moisture that could lead to higher humidity, more clouds and increased opportunities for showers and thunderstorms across parts of the region. Depending on exactly how the pattern evolves, locally heavy rainfall could also become a concern. However, it remains too early to determine whether Marie itself will produce any direct impacts in California or the Southwest. There is still considerable spread among the forecast models regarding the eventual track and how close the system could get to the region. Forecast uncertainty remains high, especially since the system has not developed a well-defined center yet. Until a consolidated circulation forms, models are essentially trying to forecast the future track of a center that does not fully exist. Confidence should begin to increase once the main center forms and models have a better starting point. This will be an important system to watch closely through the week as Labor Day weekend approaches⚠️🌀🌧️

🌡️ 4-Factor FeelsLike Forecast 🌡️ 
It’s the feels-like in Sun and Wind!
The US heat this week will be extreme. 
Traditional heat index forecasts do NOT include the sun and wind. Odd right? I’ve always thought they should because some folks spend so much time exposed. So, I found a formula from Dr. Robert Steadman in a white paper, and it turns out one version is being used by the Australian Bureau of Meteorology right now. This 4-factor equation I’m using takes both into account. Sun spikes it. In sunny spots the sun adds ~ 15°! Generally wind cools it. For instance: Nashville in the shade is 105. Raleigh in the shade feels like 102. DC in the shade is 100. Atlanta in the shade is 97. Bottom line you can NOT directly compare this to our NOAA traditional heat index, and it should not be used to replace it. It does illustrate how being in the summer Sun makes a dramatic difference. So… shade is your friend this week. Be safe!!

items.author: MeteorologistChristopherNunley
items.text: TROPICAL MOISTURE COULD SURGE INTO SOUTHERN CALIFORNIA NEXT WEEKEND🌴🌀🌧️ there are growing signals that tropical moisture could make a significant push northward into Southern California next weekend into early the following week, potentially bringing heavy rain, increased humidity, thunderstorms and strong south swells. A developing tropical disturbance off Mexico currently has a 90% chance of becoming a tropical cyclone within the next seven days. While it is far too early to know the eventual track or whether the tropical system itself gets anywhere near California, a notable number of ensemble and deterministic model solutions show the system - or a substantial plume of its moisture - being pulled northward from near Baja California toward Southern California. By next Sunday, the average precipitable water value among ensemble members climbs to around 1.5 inches, with several individual members exceeding 2 inches. Those would represent very high moisture levels for Southern California and could support periods of heavy rainfall if the necessary atmospheric lift develops. The evolving upper-level pattern will be critical. A cut-off low may linger near Northern California into the weekend, disrupting the typical subtropical ridge that often keeps tropical systems and their moisture confined farther south. If the trough remains near the West Coast, it could effectively open the door for tropical moisture to recurve northward toward California. There remains considerable uncertainty. Ensemble guidance still varies significantly regarding the position of the West Coast trough, the Southern Rockies ridge and the eventual tropical cyclone. Small changes in this pattern could mean the difference between deep tropical moisture reaching California or remaining largely offshore. For now, there is at least a chance of precipitation across Southern California next weekend, but confidence in exact rainfall amounts and locations remains low. This is not a forecast for a tropical cyclone landfall in California. The bigger concern at this stage is the possibility of a substantial tropical moisture surge producing heavy rain, thunderstorms, muggy tropical conditions and strong south swells. With roughly a week to go, expect plenty of changes in the forecast🌴🌀🌧️

items.author: MeteorologistChristopherNunley
items.text: FALL-LIKE STORM TO BRING RAIN, WIND & VERY HIGH-ELEVATION SNOW TO THE PACIFIC NORTHWEST THIS WEEK🌧️💨❄️a significant change to fall-like weather is increasingly likely across the Pacific NorthwestWednesday through Friday as a deep upper-level low and strong cold front move into the region. Widespread rain, gusty winds, much cooler temperatures and even some snow on the highest Cascade peaks are expected. Wednesday into Thursday currently looks like the wettest period, with widespread wetting rain likely from Washington through Oregon. The heaviest totals are favored along the coast, Coast Range, Olympics and Cascades. Parts of southwest Washington and northwest Oregon have a high likelihood of exceeding 1 inch of rain over a 48-hour period, with locally 2-3 inches or more possible in the higher terrain. Rainfall amounts will generally decrease farther inland, but rain should still reach portions of eastern Washington and Oregon. Showers linger into Friday. Gusty southerly winds will accompany the front Wednesday, particularly along the Washington and Oregon coasts, Northwest Interior and east of the Cascades. Some areas of eastern Washington could see gusts around 30-40 mph. While winds in western Washington may remain below typical advisory thresholds, impacts could be greater than the wind speeds alone suggest. Trees are still carrying full foliage, and some have been stressed by the dry summer, increasing the potential for isolated power outages and tree or branch damage. Much colder air will also arrive behind the front and with the upper low, with snow levels potentially falling to around 7,000 feet in the northern Washington Cascades Wednesday night and remaining relatively low through late week. This would mainly bring snow to the highest peaks rather than the mountain passes, but it will be another noticeable sign of the approaching seasonal transition. There will also be a low-end chance of thunderstorms across parts of the region Wednesday and Thursday. Any stronger showers or thunderstorms could produce brief heavy rain, lightning, small hail and locally gusty winds. Temperatures will tumble well below normal, with some areas running 10-20°F below normal. The rain may not completely end fire season, but widespread wetting rainfall and cooler conditions should provide meaningful relief and help slow ongoing wildfire activity🌧️💨❄️

items.author: MattDevittWeather
items.text:
🌀 TROPICAL UPDATE: Chances are increasing for Tropical Storm #Edouard to briefly form in the Gulf early this week. I’m also watching the remnants of #Dolly. Here's the latest and what to know:

1) INVEST 97L: This is the area in the northern Gulf we are currently invest-igating (how it gets that Invest label). Today it has been getting its act together with increasing storm coverage and what appears to be a closed surface circulation. Right now, the NHC has bumped up development odds to 50% as of 2 PM Sunday, but respectfully, I feel that is too low based on recent observations. 

If trends continue, the Gulf could see a short-lived Tropical Depression or Tropical Storm #Edouard along with a cone here soon. Hurricane Hunters will be flying into the system starting Monday morning. In its projected path westward, water temperatures are warmer than average and wind shear will be pretty low, which would favor organization and strengthening. What will be working against the system will be dry air and time. It’ll be pushing onshore along the SE Texas or SW Louisiana coast on Tuesday. Even if it forms, it doesn’t appear to be a big or powerful storm, but ironically, smaller storms have historically shown that they can strengthen (or weaken) quickly. Impacts may be limited, but it'll still be capable of heavy rain / pockets of flooding, gusty wind, higher tides and even a tornado threat. 

2) REMNANTS OF DOLLY: Passing by Puerto Rico today and bringing scattered rain and storms to the area. They need every drop, 44% of the island is currently experiencing a Level 4 “Extreme” drought. The remnants of Dolly also brought winds gusts as high as 60 mph to the island of Saba in the Caribbean this morning. 

From here, it’ll head towards the direction of the Bahamas, Florida and Eastern Gulf. Florida timing would be Thursday, Friday…and even as late as the Labor Day weekend. I would think of it as Thursday (earliest) and Labor Day (latest) depending on track, which still has a big range. Biggest question that still needs to be answered is what will it approach as? Just a rainmaker with a lot of tropical moisture helping to increase rain chances? Or will it be a tropical system? Some models do show the potential for #Dolly to reform (it would still keep that name), but not all do. As a result, the current odds for development from the NHC are at 20% as of Sunday afternoon Regardless of what it becomes, Florida needs more rain!   

I'll continue to keep you updated 24/7 with no hype, just the facts. Thanks everyone!

- Matt Devitt Weather

items.text: PNW EARLY-SEASON WIND RISK WEDNESDAY💨🌲🌧️🍂a strong-for-early-September storm system will move into the Pacific Northwest on Wednesday, bringing widespread rain along with increasingly gusty winds! Across western Washington, western Oregon and northwestern California, the strongest winds are currently favored along the coast and in Washington, the Northwest Interior as a cold front approaches and eventually moves through Wednesday into Wednesday night. Although wind alerts may not be issued, this system could still produce more impacts than the numbers alone would suggest. One important factor is that the trees still have their full summer foliage. Leaves significantly increase the surface area exposed to the wind, putting additional stress on branches and entire trees. Combine that with trees already stressed or weakened following a dry summer, and it may take less wind than during a typical late-fall or winter storm to cause problems. As a result, isolated power outages and some downed or broken tree branches will be possible Wednesday, particularly where the strongest gusts occur. A few weakened tree branches could also come down. There remains uncertainty regarding the exact track and strength of the system, which will ultimately determine how strong the winds become. Right now, this does not look like a major Pacific Northwest windstorm, but it is an early-season system worth watching closely because of the increased vulnerability of fully leafed and drought-stressed trees. Rain, gusty winds and much cooler temperatures will make Wednesday feel much more like fall across the region💨🌲🌧️🍂

What does “Ring of Fire” mean?

No, it doesn’t mean everything is literally on fire.

In weather, a “Ring of Fire” pattern happens when a large ridge of high pressure sets up and produces intense heat underneath it. Storm systems are often forced to travel around the outer edge of that heat dome, basically tracing a ring around it.

For us, the big story to start September looks to be the HEAT. Temperatures could soar well into the 90s and potentially near 100° at times during the first 10 days of the month.

The good news? These patterns eventually break down, and September is typically when we start watching for those first stronger pushes of cooler air.

So hang in there… summer isn’t finished with us just yet! 🥵

A multi-day severe weather event could kick off Tuesday across parts of the Northeast!

An upper-level disturbance pivoting out of the Great Lakes will track along the edge of a strong ridge and collide with a very warm, humid airmass. Soundings indicate elongated and curved hodographs, which indicates that wind shear will be favorable for a few supercellular structures to develop. Any stronger storms that get organized will be capable of producing damaging wind gusts, hail, and potentially an isolated tornado. 

Morning cloud cover could create localized heating boundaries that alter where storms develop, so there could be changes to the slight risk's location as we get closer to Tuesday.
